title: The font at the door
hook: some churches put the font by the door: you enter by baptism

segments.voice: Yesterday, table, pulpit, font: where a church puts its furniture shows what it puts first. Your line was what's at the center. What did you find at the center of your own rooms? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

Rain on her coat, a woman comes in off the street. Before she's taken two steps, her hand goes out to a small stone basin fixed to the wall. She dips her fingertips, touches her forehead, her chest, one shoulder, the other, and walks on without breaking stride. Behind her, a father lifts a small boy up so he can reach the water too. The boy splashes more than he dips. In other churches, the big font itself, the basin where people are baptized, stands right inside the entrance, so that everyone who comes in has to walk past it. Water first. Then the rest of the church. Today: the font at the door.

Some churches put the font at the door for a reason you can say in one sentence: in Christian teaching, a person enters the church by baptism. The building says it with its floor plan. Start with the entrance. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus, "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Enter is the word. So the water sits where you enter. Next, what the water means. In Romans, Paul describes baptism as a burial: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Down into the water, up out of it, and then you walk. In a church with the font by the door, every walk up the aisle starts beside that water. Then, the door itself. Jesus says, "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved." A font beside the door puts the two pictures side by side: the door, and the water. Last, the fingertips. Catholics dip their fingers in holy water on the way in and make the sign of the cross. Some describe it as a small reminder, every single time, of the day they were baptized. Not every church places its water at the entrance. Some baptize at the front, before the whole congregation, and some in a river. Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches baptize infants; Baptists and some others baptize those old enough to speak their own faith. Different doors, the same water.
screen: `BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch water at a door. If you can, carry a small glass of water to the doorway of the room you're in. If not, any water will do. Settle, and breathe. Dip your fingertips. Notice the temperature of the water. Touch your forehead, and let the water dry there on its own. If you pray, and it's your custom, you can make the sign of the cross, or say quietly a line from Psalm 51: wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Or simply stand in the doorway, feeling the water, before you step through. The bell holds the time.
screen: `WASH ME THROUGHLY FROM MINE INIQUITY, AND CLEANSE ME FROM MY SIN.`

segments.voice: The font at the door. Water set at a church's entrance, because in Christian teaching a person enters the church by baptism, and passes that water every time they come in.
screen: `THE FONT AT THE DOOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: enter by water. Today, the next time you come home, wash your hands first thing, slowly, and let it mark the crossing from outside to in. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door and make the sign of the cross as they enter; in some churches the baptismal font itself stands near the entrance, while others baptize at the front or in a river.

notes: The index hook says 'many churches put the font by the door'; the script says 'some churches' to keep to the claims rule.
'Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches baptize infants; Baptists and some others baptize those old enough to speak their own faith': confirm this is fair to both.
Holy water stoup custom (fingertips, sign of the cross, as a reminder of baptism) is described as Catholic practice; 'some describe it as a reminder' is attributed. Confirm.
Psalm 51:2 offered in the practice is KJV text, not a new prayer.
Hook's 'two steps' is a scene detail, not a factual count.

Editor: hook no longer opens with day 1351's 'the heavy door swings shut'; cut the claim that Paul never describes baptism as washing (compare Titus 3:5); practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
Audit (2026-10-02): pronunciation of baptizo changed to bap-TEE-zoh (English/Erasmian, as listeners will expect); a Keeper may prefer modern Greek vap-.
